Course Name: A historical perspective of Aerospace Engineering
Description: PART-I : Based on inputs from CLE (LASE program) Recommended Topics: -------------------- * The scientific revolution of the 17th century -- mechanics of the craftsmen and mathematics of the scholars are fused to explain the Universe.  * The 18th century enlightenment movement and growing dominance of the scientific worldview.  * The 19th century steam engine and electric generator, and the industrial revolution. Evolutionary perspectives in geology, biology and society. The professionalization of Science and development of its secular and elite character. * The 20th century - the birth of new physics and chemistry of the atomic and subatomic world, and related technologies. The birth of computing machines, aerodynamic and space technologies. The growing knowledge of cellular and molecular biology, and human diseases. * The 21st century - the global concerns for public health and pandemics, ecological devastation and agricultural crisis, social and economic inequality, remain and continue to grow.  PART-II : 1. History of Aerospace Engineering a. Aeronautics and Aerospace – Aircrafts and Rockets b. Basic structure/geometry/terminology of aircrafts and rockets c. Basic science of flight – Number of disciplines involved in aerospace technology d. Stories of flight – Across the world e. Evolution in flying – balloons and gliders f. Flight of heavier than air object – First flight, First rockets 2. Major milestones (discoveries and inventions) and its impact on society and industrial revolution, including negative impacts on the society. a. Global milestones – First balloon flight, powered flight, V2 rockets, Supersonic flight, civilian supersonic, Shuttle flights, SPACEX etc. b. Indian milestones – First Indigenous aircraft design- HF24, LCA, ALH, SLV, PSLV, GSLV etc. 3. Evolution of ethics and practices in the discipline – Nuclear and Chemical Weapons control, Export control laws etc. 4. Important persons, their biographies, struggle, and success. a. Indian and global 5. Voices from the field (invited talks from practitioners and professionals) – Have couple of talks every semester 6. Recent and cutting edge research in the discipline 7. Prospective directions of evolution of the discipline in the near future.

Content (List of the topics/sub-topics to be covered in the lectures/practicals/assignments): • Governing equations for compressible fluid flows – differential and integral forms, equation of states for perfect and real gasses, Reynolds and Favre averaging to deal with turbulent flow modelling. • Introduction to basics of hyperbolic partial differential equations - Characteristics, general solution and its application to linear hyperbolic system. • Properties of 1D and 2D Euler equations, elementary wave solutions, Riemann problem for Euler equations and its solutions. • Introduction to multi-dimensional finite volume method for Navier-Stokes equations – structured and unstructured grid formulations, cell centered and cell vertex approaches, static and moving grid formulations, evaluations of geometric quantities of control volume, data structures for unstructured grid computations, discretization of convective and viscous fluxes, temporal discretization, grid movement algorithms, stability conditions. • Development of upwind methods based on flux difference splitting – approximate Riemann solvers for 1D Euler equations, rotational invariance property and extension of Riemann solvers for 2D finite volume formulations, concept of genuinely multidimensional Riemann solver. • Higher order temporal and spatial discretizations in finite volume formulations; spurious oscillations, monotonicity, positivity, total variations diminishing, local extremum diminishing criteria, development of non-linear discretization techniques for non-oscillatory solutions. Description: Course Objectives: To expose students to the history of civil engineering and role in building human civilisations. To expose students to the fundamentals of civil engineering relevant to challenges faced by society in the 21st century. To inspire students for leadership and excellence in their professional careers. To expose students regarding societal-scale and global challenges involving civil engineering domain with innovative, often multi-disciplinary, solutions. Learning Outcomes: An overall understanding of requirements of sustainable design of future infrastructure systems, particularly in the context of India’s rapid urbanization and growth. An ability to identify, formulate, and solve complex engineering problems by applying principles of engineering, science, and mathematics. Sensitivity towards challenges in infrastructure systems. An ability to apply engineering design to produce solutions that meet specified needs with consideration of public health, safety, and welfare, as well as global, cultural, social, environmental, and economic factors. An ability to function in a team and communicate effectively with a range of audiences (peers, PDFs, instructors). An ability to recognize ethical and professional responsibilities in engineering situations and make informed judgments, which must consider the impact of engineering solutions in global, economic, environmental, and societal contexts. Hands-on experience on design and implementation of innovative solutions including collection, analysis and interpretation of data, use of relevant state-of-art tools and engineering judgment to draw conclusions. Course Content: History, importance and success of Civil Engineering; Science & Engineering before medieval period; The scientific revolution of the 17th century -- mechanics of the craftsmen and mathematics of the scholars are fused to explain the Universe; The 18th century enlightenment movement and growing dominance of the scientific worldview. The 19th century steam engine and electric generator, and the industrial revolution. Evolutionary perspectives in geology, biology and society. The professionalization of Science and development of its secular and elite character; The 20th century - the birth of new physics and chemistry of the atomic and subatomic world, and related technologies. The birth of computing machines, aerodynamic and space technologies. The growing knowledge of cellular and molecular biology, and human diseases; The 21st century - the global concerns for public health and pandemics, ecological devastation and agricultural crisis, social and economic inequality, remain and continue to grow; Global urbanisation trends (Eg., ASCE Future Vision 2070, GIFT City, Amravathi, etc.); Planning process & their components (incl. problem identification); Future society requirements for sustainable growth – Rapid urbanisation, India’s urban future, Growth to ensure sustenance & sustainability; Societal, economic, developmental and technical considerations and their intersections; Infrastructure development; Identification of challenges – built environment, transportation, water/waste water and energy systems; Introduction to state-of-art tools for design of intelligent infrastructure; Prototyping and innovative solutions to the identified challenges; Group projects/Hackathons on select topics; Expert talks.

Course Objectives: • To introduce students to the different types of data in civil engineering and how to process them. • To expose students to the fundamentals of learning from data relevant to civil engineering. • To inspire students to harness developments in artificial intelligence, machine learning and data science to understand and solve civil engineering problems. • To inspire students to implement data-driven modeling for infrastructure systems in a computer programming environment for futuristic civil engineering challenges. Learning Outcomes: • An overall understanding of data types relevant to civil engineering, particularly in the context of intelligent systems. • An ability to identify, formulate and solve complex civil engineering problems by applying principles of artificial intelligence, machine learning and data science. • An ability to implement data-driven modeling to address futuristic civil engineering challenges using a computer programming environment. • An ability to function in a team and communicate effectively with a range of audiences. • An ability to infer from data for knowledge enhancement, as well as civil engineering design, planning and management. • Hands-on experience on analysis and interpretation of civil engineering data, and use of relevant state-of-art machine learning tools to draw conclusions. Course Content: • Introduction to data-driven systems and examples from different fields of civil engineering, semantics and definitions of artificial intelligence and machine learning, different types and sources of data. • Introduction to linear models, simple and multiple linear regression, logistic regression, k-Nearest Neighbors approach. • Supervised Learning – Classification and Regression Part I: Decision trees and Support Vector Machines. Definition and types of neurons, neural network architecture, cost function, feed forward back propagation algorithm, multiclass classification, neural networks for regression, introduction to deep learning. • Unsupervised Learning Part I: Clustering. Definition of clustering, different distance measures, introduction to hierarchical and partitional clustering, k-means clustering, cluster validity indices, introduction to fuzzy logic and fuzzy c-means clustering. • Unsupervised Learning Part II: Multivariate Analysis and Dimension Reduction. Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Empirical Orthogonal Functions (EOF). • Group projects/research on select topics.

This course will teach students how to think about problems in transport phenomena. This course will deal with theory, tools and techniques for estimation of process states (variables) in the presence of uncertainty. This uncertainty is in the form of uncertainty (noise) in measurements as well as disturbances/noise in the process. The theory covered will deal with estimation for dynamic systems for both linear and nonlinear processes, as well as for gaussian and non-gaussian noise characteristics. Issues related to constraints on process states (constrained estimation), and delayed and multirate measurements will also be dealt with. It is expected that this course will expose the student to not only the well-accepted basics of estimation, but also to recent advances in this area. Throughout the course, the main ideas will be illustrated using matlab-based examples. The following topics will be covered: (i) Linear Optimal (Kalman) Filtering: Least squares formulation, Stochastic formulation, Riccatti equation and solution techniques, Sensitivity and sub-optimal filtering, Smoothing. (ii) Nonlinear Filtering with Gaussian Noise: Extended Kalman filtering, Unscented Kalman filtering. (iii) Particle Filtering: Sequential Monte-Carlo (SMC) methods, Markov processes, SMC based particle filtering, Resampling-MOVE algorithm, Importance sampling, SMC based smoothing, Self organizing state space models, Regularization in particle filtering. Course Name: Machine Learning for Climate and Sustainability
Description: Unit 1: A basic forward-backward optimization loop : In this unit we will setup a simple neural network that learns logic gates using logistic regression. The purpose of this simple exercise will be to familiarize ourselves with pytorch, how to implement the training and validation loops, and get an intuition for how the network learns. Unit 2: Identifying climate patterns from data : We will employ principal component analysis (PCA) to identify prominent modes of variability in the ocean-atmosphere system. We will isolate and identify modes of variability like El Nino and Indian Ocean Dipole from raw ocean data. Unit 3: Using deep neural networks for prediction tasks In this unit we will use an artificial neural network to learn relationships between hazards and their drivers. We will see that different drivers might be important in different regions. Unit 4: Gap filling of data : Satellite-derived datasets inevitably have gaps in them. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been shown to perform well on many vision tasks. We will use CNNs to fill such gaps in satellite-derived datasets. Unit 5: Emulating numerical models with neural operators : In this unit we will extend CNNs to state-of-the-art architectures like neural operators. We will emulate the three dimensional oceanic or atmospheric circulation using one such neural operator.

Description: Recent applications of ML (recommendation systems, NLP, RL etc) requiresolving large scale problems. Parallelism detection - data dependence, direction vectors, loop carried and loop independent dependences; tests for data dependence and their applicability, construction of data dependence graph. (5) Image restoration: * image degradations; * methods for image denoising, deblurring; * image quality evaluation metrics. (6) Frequency-domain processing: * Fourier transforms and their properties; * sampling theorem; * applications in image filtering. (7) Image compression: * coding, entropy; * JPEG; * multiscale image representations. (8) Morphological image processing. (9) Principal component analysis and applications in image processing, e.g., eigenfaces. (10) Deep neural networks for image processing: * neural network architectures; * loss functions and learning methods; * applications.

Intention is to cover a reasonable subset of the following topics. Continuous and Discrete Optimization are two important pillars of machine learning. Continuous optimization typically occurs in learning model parameters while discrete optimization problems appear in inference and auxiliary tasks such as feature selection, data subset selection, model compression etc. In the first part of this course, we will cover continuous optimization with applications in machine learning. Topics to discuss will include Convexity, Gradient Methods, Proximal algorithms, Stochastic and Online Variants of mentioned methods, Coordinate Descent Methods, Subgradient Methods, Non-Convex Optimization, FrankWolfe, Accelerated Methods, Lagrange and Fenchel Duality, Second-Order Methods, Quasi-Newton Methods, Gradient-Free and Zero-Order Optimization. We will also cover some advanced topics including non-convex optimization, alternating minimization algorithms and parallel/distributed variants of algorithms. We will ground all these algorithms with applications and loss functions in machine learning (starting from logistic regression, linear regression, svms, matrix factorization right up to deep neural networks). Summarily,in Continuous Optimization we will cover topics such as Basics of Continuous Optimization, Convexity, Gradient Descent, Projected/Proximal GD, Subgradient Descent, Accelerated Gradient Descent, Newton & Quasi Newton, Duality: Legrange, Fenchel, Coordinate Descent, Frank Wolfe, Continuous Optimization in Practice, etc. The second part of this course will cover the fundamentals of discrete optimization. We will start with basic forms of combinatorial optimization (knapsack, s-t cuts/paths, matchings and matroids) and then discuss submodular functions and their applications. We will cover algorithms for submodular minimization and maximization under various combinatorial constraints. We will also discuss discrete probabilistic models such as Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs). We will ground all these algorithmic and theoretical results with real world applications in feature selection, summarization and diversified search, structured prediction, data subset selection and model compression. The energy industry is seeing an influx of data from new ICT and IOT interventions, leading to several problem statements seeking data-driven solutions. The problems span a wide gamut - from forecasting to pattern recognition, from anomaly detection to predictive maintenance and from cost minimization to efficiency optimization to name a few. This course can provide an introductory platform to the evolving world of energy informatics to interested students. Moreover, this course is ideally suited to introduce project/activity-based learning in the Electrical Engineering curriculum. It is an excellent sequel to the newly introduced AI and data science course EE 353, allowing students to apply the techniques learnt in that course to industry inspired problems. The course will also bring in industry professionals to provide insights on real world problems and also to evaluate the innovative solutions designed during the course. This way, the course is designed to produce well rounded energy data analysts much needed today. Module 1 (Introduction to energy data analytics and energy systems):Introduction to energy data analytics, focusing on the importance of data in theenergy sector. Overview of the key sources of energy data (smart meters,sensors, satellite data, etc.) and the typical tools and programming languages(Python, R, SQL, etc.) used for energy data analytics. Brief overview of energysystems, including generation, transmission, and distribution networks;renewable/conventional energy sources; consumption patterns and gridoperations.Module 2 (Data Processing and Exploratory Analysis): Data acquisition fromIoT devices, SCADA, and APIs. Data cleaning and preprocessing techniques(handling missing values and outliers). Time series analysis in energy data.Correlation between different energy variables. Pattern identification andanomaly detection. Typical machine learning applications in energy domain(demand forecasting, anomaly detection, consumer clustering, etc).Module 3 (Overview of various data-driven applications in energy domain):Forecasting energy demand and supply using time series techniques (ARIMA,SARIMA, LSTMs); Impact of weather on energy demand; Considerations inlong-term/medium-term/short-term forecasting.Optimization and decision support systems for energy efficiency optimization,demand-side management, building automation and control, energy costminimization and system control.Use of data for energy market analysis and policy studies, including electricitypricing models, carbon footprint analysis, energy transition studies.Overview of phasor measurement units and wide-area monitoring and control forpower grids.Role of IoT in smart energy systems (buildings cities, grids etc), big datatechniques for handling large-scale energy datasets, Cloud and edge computingapplications.Case studies and industry applications (examples include energy theft detection,power purchase cost optimization, power management in data centers)

Course Name: Crystalline Silicon Solar Cells: Theory and Practice
Description: Module 1: Theory: Brief review of semiconductor device physics - band structure - carrier concentrations - carrier generation and recombination - effective lifetime and surface recombination velocity - carrier transport - optical absorption and reflection. Practice: (i) measurement of sheet resistance of a silicon wafer - determination of the type of wafer - estimation of the mobility and diffusion coefficient of the majority carriers (ii) measurement of carrier lifetime and surface recombination velocity (iii) measurement of reflectivity of a polished silicon surface. Module 2: Theory: p-n junction diodes - derivation of dark IV characteristics including surface recombination - illuminated IV characteristics - contacts - series resistance in solar cells - shunts in solar cells. Practice: Simulation of dark and illuminated IV characteristics of pn junction diodes using PC1D - analysis of fermi levels, potential, electric field and carrier distributions, generation and recombination rates within the diode - simulation of illuminated characteristics using measured reflectance data - leakage currents - impact of various parameters like carrier lifetime, surface recombination, and semiconductor thickness on carrier distributions, recombination currents and dark and illuminated IV of the diode, impact of the above on solar cell performance parameters (Isc, Voc, FF, efficiency). Module 3: Theory: wet clean and etch processes - Diffusion in silicon - plasma etching - thin film growth and deposition (oxidation, PECVD, ALD, evaporation), screen printing process - laser processes for silicon solar cell fabrication Practice: Texturization of silicon surface using KOH, measurement of reflectance, observation of the surface using optical microscope and assessment of pyramid size and distribution, review of device simulation using the measured reflectance data - Phosphorous diffusion using POCl3, design of diffusion process - experiment, sheet resistance measurements - edge isolation process using plasma etching, characterization of edge isolation - PECVD nitride deposition, ellipsometry to determine thickness, reflectance measurements, lifetime measurements - review of simulation using experimentally measured data - screen printing and firing, measurement of linewidths using optical microscope, measurement of bus bar sheet resistance, contact resistance measurements using TLM techniques as applied on solar cell - review of simulations. Module 4: Theory: Design and analysis of solar cells - minimization of optical losses - minimization of recombination losses - quantum efficiency measurements - loss analysis of solar cells Practice: Design and analysis of solar cells using Al-BSF technology, use experimentally determined parameters from previous section to design cells, PC1D and other software like PV light house can be used - fabrication of solar cells with Al-BSF - measurement of solar cell characteristics - discussion of IEC60904, simulation of spectrum as a function of environmental conditions - analysis of dark and illuminated IV - quantum efficiency measurements - analysis of losses in the solar cell - review of simulations.

Course Name: Energy Storage: Technology, Grid Application, and Economics
Description: In order to address climatic issues, the world is experiencing energy transition from conventional fossil fuel-based system to clean and sustainable energy system. In the journey of energy transition, power sector is experiencing most rapid transition through renewable energy integration across the world, particularly solar and wind power. However, intermittent and variable nature of solar PV and wind power is introducing a range of challenges in power sector, including resource adequacy issues, overgeneration during high solar hours (duck curve etc.), stability issues, supply demand balance during low RE generation scenarios, lack of flexible resources, and various other challenges to provide reliable and resilient RE dominated electricity supply. Energy storage is evolving as one of the primary interventions to address the above stated issues in RE integrated system and enable generation firming capacity for reliable electricity supply. In India, energy storage capacity requirement is projected to be 83 GWh (48 GWh from pumped storage plants and 35 GWh from Battery) for year 2026-27. Energy storage requirement in India is further expected to increase to 415 GWh by 2031-32. Ministry of Power has projected that by the year 2047, the requirement of energy storage is expected to increase to 2380 GWh due to the addition of a larger scale renewable energy in light of the net zero emissions targets set for 2070. Therefore, considering pressing need for innovative energy storage technologies in the power sector, this course is aimed to train the students with energy storage technology, its application and emerging storage technologies for seamless integration of renewables, thereby preparing for increasing and pressing need of skilled manpower required for the sector.

Description: ENT602 Technology Venture Creation: The purpose of this capstone course is to enable students to work on product development and startupbusiness plan of technology led entrepreneurial opportunities. It will help students get hands-on experience on the process of product development and start-up formation. Students are expected to develop the leadership skills required to begin their entrepreneurial journey. Description: "The field of Entrepreneurship is increasingly important for India as evidenced by policy push for universities as also other sections of the society through the Startup India initiative. Popular research has identified that among various reasons for failure of new ventures, incorrect identification of customer need and problem statement is by far the most prevalent. This course will aid aspiring entrepreneurs (typically B Tech / MTech /PhD students) in deep understanding of customer needs and pain points thus eliminating the waste that occurs. For doctoral students, ethnographic enquiry is a well established methodology for theory building endeavours. With the field of entrepreneurship veering towards 302221entrepreneurship as practice302222 , a sociological approach to understanding this domain, field immersion techniques become crucial from academic research perspective. This methodology which forms the bedrock of theory building is particularly important at the time that India specific theories in the field of entrepreneurship are being sought to better promote new ventures in the economy.""1) Ethnography as a methodology for Innovation & entrepreneurship practice and research2) Gaining access to the field and ethics of ethnographic inquiry3) Participant and Non participant observations4) Forms of data - Visual data, historical data, videos and articles5) Data Collection - conducting Ethnographic interviews, shadowing the protagonists, artefacts6) Data Storage and organization7) Field notes and thick description8) Open and Axial Coding"

Description: This course offers an introduction to the 1) impact of AI on startups and businesses, and 2) the emergence of new AI startups. Students will learn how AI is useful for businesses, and analyse the kind of functions and areas where AI may be applied. Students will learn how AI driven data feed into decision-making and more efficient processes. The course will also discuss how to think about the impact of AI implementation, and what leadership means in a rapidly changing AI-driven scenario. Students will learn about the pitfalls of AI including working with low-quality data, and ethical implications of Gen AI. In this course we will cover the following aspects: 1. Introduction to Gen AI and the AI landscape and why it is important for businesses to look at and understand AI. 2. Examples and use cases of how AI is applied in different business functions and sectors. How AI tools can be used in common business domains, functions and processes, how AI-driven data feeds into decision-making. We look at AI implementation examples in different business functions. 3. New business opportunities emerging out of AI and emerging AI first business. 4. Impact of AI on industries and sectors 5. Responsible AI: Ethics, Bias, Regulation 6. Role of leadership and change management: how to lead and manage AI-driven change.

Course Name: Advanced topics in deep learning for image analysis
Description: The course will deal with advanced deep learning techniques used to solve critical inference problems in remote sensing, image analysis, and computer vision. We plan to cover the following learning paradigms which consider learning a classification model under different levels of supervision. Meta- learning and few-shot learning Zero-shot learning Self-supervised learning Multi-modal learning Multi-task learning Continual learning Domain adaptation and generalization Uncertainty estimation in deep learning We will consider the application of the aforementioned learning algorithms for visual inference tasks with focus to image classification and semantic segmentation. To this end, land-cover classification from remote sensing images of varied modalities would be the running application example that will be discussed at length for all the algorithms. In addition, we will consider a few challenging classification problems in remote sensing (cross-sensor data retrieval, change detection, and land cover map generation for geographically disjoint and large areas) and show how some of these learning techniques (domain adaptation, uncertainty estimate) can be modified to solve these problems. Finally, annotation is a major problem in remote sensing, we plan to discuss how off-the-shelves self-supervision can be used as an alternative in this regard. Like the examples from the remote sensing area, we will consider examples from natural image and video analysis literature concerning very large-scale datasets (ImageNet, DomainNet, to name a few).

Course objective: The understanding of human physiological and psychological functions is one of the most useful and beneficial assets in a technological and industrial environment. It is for better management of human life that one must have a good understanding of human behaviour, thoughts and feelings. Among these, stress is one of the most common psycho-physiological phenomena of today and moreover, the young have been found to be its usual victims. In fact, stress and its emotional components result from the complex interaction of genetic, physiological, behavioural, and environmental factors, which finally disturb the homeostasis (balance among internal physiological conditions) of the body. This course is designed to cover the entire field of enquiry as given above. Course outline: Fundamentals of behavioural health. Behavioural health and industrial hazards, health aspects related to personality (focus on Type-A personality pattern, converted Type-A persons who are a great challenge of the 21st century), perception and emotionality. Drug addiction and rehabilitation. Alcoholism and other substance abuse. Understanding stress and its various causes. Stress and psychologically-oriented and physically-manifested disorders [Psychosomatic disorders] Manic depressive tendencies, socialization problems, eating disorders. Depression and other related psychological states that are also manifest in the technological/industrial environment. Stress and adjustment :Occupational, social, marital, sexual and environmental aspects. Technology and subjective well-being (SWB)

Course Name: History as a Discipline: Elementary Concepts
Description: This course intends to introduce history as a discipline to undergraduate students. While students have read the histories of particular places, times and objects at school (and thus history is not a new subject), they will benefit by learning the ideational processes whereby the study of history got instituted as a compulsory component of school-level education across the world since the nineteenth century. The course is thus a history of ideas that have had a global currency in modern times. Specifically, it delves into the history of the institutionalization of the modern discipline of history. It will probe into why the nineteenth and twentieth century world has often been described as the most historically minded of all ages. In doing so, the course will draw out the differences between the ‘post-Renaissance sense of the past’ and older conceptions of history (the history of Herodotus, Thucydides, for example, or the itihasa-purana traditions of India). A part of the course will, in fact, explore in depth these older traditions. The focus will be on early Indian traditions of engaging with the past—the many facets of itihasa in the long history of the Indian subcontinent. Literary traditions in India go back to more than two millennia: royal biographies, inscriptions, genealogies, chronicles.Thus, the subcontinent had produced numerous texts of recognizable historical intent and value. The term itihasa-purana, referring to that which was believed to have happened in the past,is mentioned in Vedic literature from early to mid-first millennium BC. Itihasa, itivritta, gatha, purana, akhyayika, udaharana, carita, vamsavali, etc. find place of prominence in Brahmanic, Buddhist and Jaina traditions. Jinasena, the ninth century Jaina author of the Adipurana, defines itihasa as relating that which actually happened. There were also changes in the genre of texts associated with itihasa. Besides the itihasa purana traditions, there were the Sramanic and bardic traditions of historical engagement in early India. Comparing with these diverse traditions of historical thinking, the course will familiarize students with how, with the onset of modernity, a rupture was brought about in the dominant definition of history and historical consciousness. This was also the time that history as a formal course of study was introduced into universities (that is, as part of school and college education). A separation was now fastidiously drawn between myth and history; between the supernatural and the natural; and between natural history and human history. As per this distinction, human history was to do only with events consciously actuated and influenced by human-beings. The course has two broad focus areas. One is the process of historical knowledge formation: how the practitioners of the discipline of history reconstruct the past. The other is the exploration of the shifts and turns in the debates on the relation between the natural sciences on the one hand, and humanities and history on the other. The philosophers of the Enlightenment conceived of history as a science—the science of evolution of society. They believed in the ideal of a unified system of all sciences, natural and humane. Another strain of thought, which became predominant in the field of history from the late nineteenth-early-twentieth century, effected a fundamental chasm between human history and the natural sciences. The ‘man-made’ came to be understood as distinctly different from the ‘natural’. The former demanded understanding from the historian, who was supposed to have an inside-view of the matter by entering the minds of the historical actors, while the latter, it was assumed, could be studied only through external observation. beings.The course has two broad focus areas. The other is the exploration of the shifts and turns in the debates on the relation between the natural sciences on the one hand, and humanities and history on the other. The philosophers of the Enlightenment conceived of history as a science—the science of evolution of society. They believed in the ideal of a unified system of all sciences, natural and humane. Another strain of thought, which became predominant in the field of history from the late nineteenth-early-twentieth century, effected a fundamental chasm between human history and the natural sciences. The ‘man-made’ came to be understood as distinctly different from the ‘natural’.The former demanded understanding from the historian, who was supposed to have an inside-view of the matter by entering the minds of the historical actors, while the latter, it was assumed,could be studied only through external observation. In the era of Anthropogenic climate change, this distinction gets obfuscated as human action has impacted the biosphere. History thus faces a novel task: its tradition of resolving questions of justice and morality and capacity for empathetic understanding have perhaps to be extended to the entire world of natural reproductive life. The course will benefit students by laying out some basic lines of convergences, unities and tensions between the sciences and the humanities, on the one hand, and between diverse pre-modern/ non-modern sensibilities about the past and a hegemonic modern sensibility, on the other. Content: 1. Unit 1: Pre-modern traditions of engaging with the past. We will focus on the many facets of the itihasa purana traditions in the Indian subcontinent. (See elaboration in the above section.) The module will explore the forms and contents of these genres. 2. Unit 2: The global discourse around history since the nineteenth century. In an era of unprecedented, rapid and dramatic historical transformation that characterized the world since the onset of the Industrial Revolution, history could no longer be simply the model or precedent for the present, as it sometimes functioned before. In this unit, we study the concept of scientific history in the nineteenth century which saw history as laying bare the direction, mechanism and laws of human evolution. Generalized patterns of rise and fall, growth and decay, progress and decline of civilizations; of the evolution of governments and governance, of economic development, etc. were sought to be mapped in the same manner in which geological and biological evolution were being researched. In this unit, we study the concept of empiricism in history—how the supposed assumptions of science were transferred to the social sciences. 3. Unit 2: The historian’s craft—on how methods of writing the past evolved through the turn of the centuries; the processes of condensation, realignment and selection in the reconstruction of the past; the relations between the present and the past; the historian and his facts; the nature of historical evidence, etc. The Collingwoodian concept of the historian as ‘actor’ and not just ‘spectator’—‘entering the minds of another’; imaginative understanding versus explanation; the problem of historical interpretation. 4. Unit 3: “Two cultures”? History and Science—the many debates across the last three centuries over the relations between the study of human history and the study of nature.between the study of human history and the study of nature. 5. Unit 4: Rethinking History in the time of anthropogenic climate change. Certain fundamental ideas about what human-beings can cause/ make or cannot cause/ make have undergone radical revision in the era of global warming.The geophysical agency of human beings is an unprecedented concept. Human history is thus getting re-conceptualized at present. This module focuses of this current rethinking of history. The history of modernity becomes the history of human ecological overreach by grave proportions. The certitudes of human history—of progress, technological mastery over nature, etc.—get unsettled when juxtaposed against the history of natural life on the planet.

Description: The course will have three core sections: 1. Archaeology, Landscapes and the Human Past : Archaeology has long been exploring ways of understanding human-land interactions. While earlier work concentrated on how humans over time have exploited the resources on and off the landscapes, later research tried to better understand how humans perceived the landscape. This part of the course will outline some of the different perspectives in order to understand the relationship between humans, the landscape and technological changes over time. 2. Paleobiological studies and the Landscape : This segment explores how paleobiological evidence - from fossil pollen to ancient animal remains - helps reconstruct past landscapes and ecosystems. Students will learn how human activities, from early hunting to agriculture and metallurgy, left lasting imprints on biodiversity, climate, and geography over tens of thousands of years. Using case studies from Ice Age extinctions, ancient river systems, and collapsed civilizations, we will examine how landscape changes influenced natural selection and species survival. The module also introduces practical techniques like microfossil analysis and paleoenvironmental mapping to trace the deep-time dynamics between humans, climate, and the biosphere. This foundation will prepare students to critically assess both ancient and modern patterns of human-environment interaction. 3. Geospatial Technologies : Geospatial technologies offer powerful tools and techniques for archaeological studies. This module will introduce the audience about the basics of geospatial technologies especially from a data collection perspective. The topics that will be covered are: Maps and its characteristics, Land Surveying, Remote Sensing and basic geospatial analysis using open-source tools.

Our access to our city is mediated by technologies, systems, conventions and most of all, by our embodied limits. This course proposes to introduce the city as our prime repository of design problems. Its purpose is to introduce students to ways in which they can begin to understand urban problems. The city offers problems which are at once of a social and technical nature, and introducing students to this area of interdisciplinary scholarship will be helpful to them in developing their own future work.This course introduces students to the city through lectures, films and assignments. Students will learn to inquire into the city around them and the many systems which constitute it as a social and physical environment. Assignments and projects will involve field work and class work to describe, diagnose and propose interventions at a human scale.At the end of this course, students will be have learnt (a) to read the city in terms of the many systems which co-exist within it, (b) techniques of mapping urban phenomena, and (c) several theoretical and conceptual perspectives from which the city has been examined in the interdisciplinary literature

Background Virtual Reality (VR) is reshaping the creative landscape, providing a canvas that goes beyond traditional limitations. Artists are no longer confined to flat surfaces or physical materials-they can paint in the air, sculpt in 360°, and animate immersive environments. By blending traditional artistic principles with cutting-edge digital tools, VR offers a revolutionary immersive and interactive expression platform. As digital tools increasingly influence creative disciplines, this course aims to equip students with the essential skills to adapt and innovate in this evolving artistic landscape. VR technology breaks down artistic barriers, enabling fully immersive experiences that open up new avenues for creativity, self-expression, and personal growth. Course Overview: Immersive Art in VR The "Immersive Art in VR" course is designed for students eager to explore art in a new dimension. It introduces participants to industry-leading VR creative tools, allowing them to experiment with painting, sculpting, animation, and calligraphy in a fully immersive environment. Students will learn how to harness the boundless potential of VR as an artistic medium, pushing the limits of imagination, interaction, and expression. Throughout the course, students will: Learn the fundamentals of VR art creation using industry-leading tools. Explore diverse artistic styles in VR, from dynamic 3D painting to virtual sculpting and animation. Create personal projects in VR, AR, or XR, choosing an art form of interest. Collaborate on group VR art installations to push creative and technical boundaries. This program delivers a transformative learning experience by leveraging VR`s unique capabilities, fostering creativity, innovation, and emotional expression. Additionally, the course incorporates creative art therapy principles, acknowledging the power of art as a means for enhancing emotional well-being and cognitive development. Learning Outcomes Upon completion of this course, students will: Master VR-based artistic tools to create digital paintings, 3D sculptures, and interactive animations. spaces. Expand creative problem-solving skills by working in 360° virtual Develop a portfolio of VR artworks, demonstrating expertise lin immersive media. Improve spatial reasoning and artistic visualization, critical for design, gaming, and AR/VR industries. Enhance emotional well-being through expressive creativity, drawing from art therapy principles. Engage in collaborative VR projects, strengthening communication and teamwork skills. Conclusion This course is more than just a new way to create art-it`s a gateway into the future of immersive creativity. By combining VR technology with expressivę artistic techniques, students will gain practical skills in digital artistry while benefiting from the therapeutic and cognitive advantages of immersive experiences. Whether students aim to explore art professionally, enter the XR industry, or simply unlock new creative possibilities, this course provides the tools and experience to push creative boundaries in the digital age.

Evolutionary perspectives in geology, biology and society. The professionalization of Science and development of its secular and elite character. The 20th century - the birth of new physics and chemistry of the atomic and subatomic world, and related technologies. The birth of computing machines, aerodynamic and space technologies. The growing knowledge of cellular and molecular biology, and human diseases. The 21st century - the global concerns for public health and pandemics, ecological devastation and agricultural crisis, social and economic inequality, remain and continue to grow.  Overview of Thermal engineering: The thermal and fluids engineering stream deals with processes that deal with transfer of energy and motion of fluids, in both coupled and uncoupled manner. Since a significant section of mechanical engineering deals with generation of power, and almost the entirety of this power is generated by means of techniques that deal with transferring energy from some form to another form, thermal and fluids engineering plays a significant role. Besides the generation of power, most systems from mechanical engineering have to deal with either absorption or dissipation of heat, and with some or other form of fluids. Hence, the principles learnt in this stream are useful throughout the entire domain of mechanical engineering. Overview of Design engineering: The design stream deals with the conceptualization of the machine that needs to be produced. The process begins with a thorough assessment of the need of such a machine. Once the necessities are clearly ascertained, the design process in initiated involving various methodologies of analysis, such as stress analysis, thermal analysis, analysis of the kinematics and dynamics of the machine including the transfer of motion and power, an analysis of manufacturability, etc. The analysis is conducted on both the machine as a composite unit as well as its components. Finally, the drawings of the manufacturable design are created and passed on to the engineers specializing in the manufacturing stream. Overview of Manufacturing engineering: The manufacturing stream is involved with the manufacturing of components for the machines that were designed by the engineers specializing in the design stream. The process begins with identification of the proper raw materials, moves on to the choice of the machines that would be utilized for machining the components, and finally the machining process itself with its associated controls over dimensions and tolerances. Engineers in this stream are constantly attempting to innovate methodologies that allow production of the machines and their components with the best of quality, but with also with least amounts of debris and the least possible cost.

Inorganic compounds: perovskite, spinel, inverse spinel, garnet, calcite, alpha-alumina,Intermetallic compounds and ordered structures. 4) Directions in the crystal lattice; distances and angles in a 3-D lattice; lattice planes and Miller indices; Metric Tensor. Reciprocal space; reciprocal metric tensor. Stereographic projection, zones, zone axes, relationship between direct and reciprocal lattice, coordinate transformations. 5) Amorphous Materials and Special Types of Crystal - Solid Aggregates. Liquid crystals, geometry of polyhedra, icosahedral packing, quasi-crystals, incommensurate structures, foams, porous and cellular materials. 6) Tensors - Tensors: definition, coordinate transformations, dummy index notation, principal axes, crystal symmetry and property tensors, field tensors, representation quadric, second, third and fourth rank tensors. Part II: Defects (Post-midsem) 7) Point Defects - Point defects in ionic crystals and ceramics (defect classification, Kroger-Vink Notation, Defect reactions, Defect equilibria and Kroger-Vink diagrams), point defect aggregates, point defect configurations, point defects in equilibrium, radiation damage, anelasticity and point defect symmetry. 8) Dislocations - Dislocation motion, force on a dislocation, distortion in a dislocated crystal. Dislocation-dislocation interactions, atom positions close to a dislocation. 9) Dislocations in Crystals - Strain energy of a dislocation, partials and stacking faults, dislocations in ccp and hexagonal metals, dislocations in bcc crystals, dislocation in rock salt structure, dislocations in covalent solids. 10) Stacking Faults and Twinning - Stacking faults, deformation twinning, examples of twin structures in CCP, BCC and HCP metals, twinning in zinc blende, calcite and graphite, twinning elements, morphology of deformation twinning. 11) Grain Boundaries, Texture and interphase boundaries - Structure and energy of grain boundaries, interface junctions, structure and energy of surfaces, shapes of crystals and grains, interphase boundary, strained layer epitaxy.

Course Name: Materials Processing in Semiconductor Technology - I
Description: A processing overview highlighting the front-end of the line (FEOL) and back-end of the line (BEOL) processes involved in semiconductor device fabrication. Details of the following processing methods will be covered in this course: 1. Wafer fabrication by melt growth: sand to ingot to wafer, Czochralski and float zone method 2. Thermal oxidation and Si/SiO2 interface: Oxide growth kinetics, dependence of growth kinetics on processing parameters like temperature and pressure 3. Dopant diffusion: Ficks laws of diffusion. Analytical and numerical solutions. Diffusion in semi-infinite, finite and composite media, Atomistic models of diffusion. Diffusion mechanisms. Diffusion profile calculations 4. Thin film deposition: * Thermodynamics of nucleation and growth. Growth modes based on energetic considerations, epitaxy, substrate requirements for epitaxy, strain considerations, dislocations due to lattice mismatch, formation of thick films for substrates and films as the thin active layer. * Thin film deposition techniques (PVD): Thornton`s diagram, Thermal evaporation, Sputter deposition (DC, RF, pulsed DC), MBE, Pulsed Laser Deposition, e-beam evaporation * Thin film deposition techniques (CVD): boundary layer formation, gas phase diffusion profiles of precursors, gas phase reactions, surface reaction and surface diffusion rates, types of CVD: MOCVD, APCVD, ALD, etc. 5. Capstone project: The project will include evaluating the instrumentation, parameter window, advantages and disadvantages of growth methods like MOCVD, APCVD, ALD, MBE, HVPE, sputter deposition, pulsed laser deposition, etc.

*** Module I: Physical and Computational Simulation of Industrial Process Routes 1. Systems Overview: Introduction to industrial production encompassing continuous casting. multi-stage hot rolling, cold reduction, and continuous annealing cycles. 2. The Critical Gap in Laboratory Experiments: Critical reassessment of the TTT diagrams for Steels. The invalidity of (even) the CCT diagrams for industrial processing. Fundamental (technical) limitations of experiments in replicating industrial processes 2. Application of Avrami Equation for obtaining non-isothermal kinetics. 3. The significant impact of Scheil`s additivity principle along with the heat of recalescence on altering phase transformation kinetics. 4. The defining role of rate of heating and by implication the limitation of lab-based thermomechanical experiments on the Recrystallization kinetics of Steel *** Module III: Discussions on lack of simulation equipment for duplicating processes that impact important properties of steels - surface finish. Roll "Crown" in rolling mill, screw down mechanism, edgers and other equipment for removal of scales during hot rolling.

Description: This course will enable students to prototype and validate industry-grade product assembly systems by integrating automation using PLCs, sensors, and industrial communication. Mini projects emphasise hardware integration, control logic, sensing, mechanical interfacing, and system reliability in product assembly environments. The project-based lab course will cover the following content: 1. PLC-based control system design for assembly sequencing, interlocking, and state-based operation. 2. Integration of industrial sensors including proximity, optical, force, vision, and environmental sensing for assembly feedback. 3. End-effector and actuator integration covering relay modules, motor starters, servo drives, pneumatic valves, and robot-PLC coordination. 4. Industrial communication networks including Modbus, Ethernet/IP, CANopen, Profinet, and OPC-UA for multi-device integration. 5. Real-time machine status acquisition using IO mapping, encoder feedback, load cells, smart sensors, and signal conditioning. 6. PLC programming using ladder logic (LD), structured text (ST), function block diagram (FBD), and sequential function charts (SFC) for assembly workflows. 7. Design and integration of HMI dashboards for operator control, alarms, and assembly diagnostics. 8. Sensor-driven error detection strategies including debounce logic, redundancy, voting mechanisms, and fault classification.

I - Amber Shrivastava
Description: This course will expose the students to the fabrication techniques to fabricate real world products with different materials. The project-based lab course will cover the following content: 1. Precision machining using CNC turning and CNC milling, including parameter selection and quality evaluation. 2. Metal additive manufacturing covering process planning, build strategies, and post-processing steps. 3. Polymer injection molding with emphasis on mold design, processing conditions, and part quality control. 4. Composite and polymer processing using autoclave systems, including layup procedures and cure-cycle optimization. 5. Digital manufacturing workflows, including CAM integration, toolpath generation, and process monitoring. 6. Design for manufacturability across machining, additive manufacturing, molding, and composite fabrication. 7. Inspection and metrology for dimensional accuracy, surface integrity, and defect identification. 8. Integrated prototyping involving fabrication, assembly, validation, and iterative design improvements.

Description: The key objective of this course is for students to Design, Fabricate, Control & Demonstrate a palm top or table top sized robot (such as but not limited to drone, autonomous car, cart-pendulum etc.). This will include all associated aspects including Mechanical, Electrical and Algorithmic. Because of the background required, this course will have some pre-requisites on UG level Controls, Dynamics Theory Courses and Basic UG Level Electrical and Mechanical Labs.First half of the semester will have both prescribed modules and project work and second half will only have project work. During the first half semester each (three hour) lab session will have two hours of prescribed hand-on modules followed by one hour of project work. During the second half of the semester, full lab session will focus on the project work only.The hands-on prescribed module (total 7 sessions) will cover/recap key aspects of Robot Design and Control such as (1) Introduction Session (1 session): Overview of Course objective and activities to familiarize with Lab Hardware/Software, (2) Dynamics and Kinematics (2 sessions): Demonstrate principles using manipulator and/or drones, (3) Feedback Control (2 sessions): PID implementation exercise on a single motor, (4) Motion Planning (2 sessions): Motion planning exercise using a wheeled mobile robot.For the project, students will work in teams formed by the instructor randomly. Teams need to finalize their project within first few weeks under the supervision of the course instructor. Students need to brainstorm design ideas and work every week towards their project and will need to submit a short (max two pages) weekly report showing their work progress with key outputs in the week.

Description: This course will contain projects that involve hands-on application of materials science and chemistry to real world problem statements, especially involving sustainable technologies such as green energy materials, recycling, and sustainable manufacturing. Depending on the faculty offering the course, projects may range from dye sensitized solar cells, quantum dots, wearable electronics, non-destructive sensor development for structural integrity assessment, recycling of E-waste, textile, packaging material, making feedstock for 3D printing, lifecycle assessment and recycling of structural alloys. These will be carried out in groups of 2-3, with a maximum cap of 20 students per semester. Interdisciplinary participation is highly encouraged.Dye sensitized solar cells, quantum dots, wearable electronics, non-destructive sensor development for structural integrity assessment,Electrodeposition will be used to extract critical metals from e-waste and redeposit them to make electrodes for batteries and other applications.Glass melting furnace (1400oC) will be used to melt waste glass, cast into shapes that can either be used directly or utilized further for glass blowing to form it into usable shapes or for aesthetic purposes.Mini extruder may be used to process shredded waste plastic to make filaments for 3D printing, Hot press will be used to recycle polymers and textiles with use of fillers into bricks / boards for structural, acoustic, thermal insulation applications. Different waste materials may first be shredded (if needed) to prepare them for further processing.Slip casting of ceramics/clays will be carried out to produce light weight ceramic products such as crucibles, trays, plates which may be used for high temperature applications or for making clay objects for various uses.Sheet metal work bench will be used to make sheet metal components with virgin sheet metal or to repurpose sheet metal from scrap.Induction melting will be used to melt waste metal into various shapes, prepare alloys and develop an understand the practise of foundry.All the above projects will use state of the art modelling techniques for alloy and chemistry design, while deploying hands-on skills of making the actual product, and will be coupled with sensors for diagnostics of structural health monitoring of the products made. The data collected will be used for improvements in design in the next iteration.

Description: PS 643-Introduction to AI, Data, and Policy is one of the two new courses, one introductory PS643 and one advanced PS 644 which replaces the old course PS 626-AI, Data and Policy which has been running for four years as an institute elective. Course Outline Documentaries for Policy Change Week 1-2 What is a Documentary? Colonial filmsThe course opens by situating documentary filmmaking within broader historical and political contexts. Students will explore the origins of the documentary as a medium to capture "fragments ofactuality starting with early films in India such as Panorama of Calcutta (1890s) and Washing a Baby (1905). These early works serve as entry points into the study of Colonial Film-cinema made under and for empire, often used to support imperial policy and shape public perception and policy. Key screenings, including A Road in India, will help students understand the colonial gaze and its narrative control. The week introduces the Films Division of India as a postcolonial institutional counterpart, continuing the legacy of using film to frame politicalideology. Reading Camille Deprez`s The Films Division of India, 1948-1964 provides essential context on the British documentary tradition`s influence on India`s state media. Students will explore the archives on Films Division`s YouTube channel and colonialfilm.org.uk to critically engage with how visual media has historically interacted with policy objectives. Week 3-4: State Sponsored Cinema and the Nation-Building Project These weeks deepen the discussion on Films Division of India as a cultural instrument of the newly independent India. Through screenings and analyses of films like I Am 20 (based in IIT Bombayalumni) and A Few More Questions, students will examine how documentaries articulated visions of modernity, national development. and civic identity.The course will explore how the state used documentary form to influence public policy discourse on youth, education, industry, andnationhood, focusing on films that often sought to construct a unified national identity amidst socio-political diversity. Focus Filmmakers such as SNS Sastry, Pramod Pati, and Sukhdev will be studied as auteurs who negotiated state directives withpersonal and political expression. Week 5-6. The Rise of the Indian Independent DocumentaryThe shift to independent documentary filmmaking in the 1980s marks a critical turn in both form and function. Students will explore how independent filmmakers providing alternative accounts of sociopolitical realities. Special attention will be given to Cinema V303251rit303251 and observationalstyles that emphasized authenticity and minimal intervention. Screenings such as Chronicle of a Summer (1961) and Grey Gardens (1975) will inform this discussion. Week 7 Documenting Culture-Between Tradition and Modernity This module explores the use of documentary to understand and narrativize cultural change, subcultures, and disappearing traditions.Students will examine films that use avant-garde, experimental, and reflexive techniques to go beyond ethnographic realism.Screenings: Mati Manas, Siddheshwari (Mani Kaul), Lovely Villa (Avijit Mukul Kishore and Rohan Shivakumar), and Bidesia in Bambai (Surabhi Sharma) showcase how filmmakers representurbanization, migration, and cultural memory within changing policy environments. These films offer new ways to visualize the intersections of culturalpolicy, heritage, and the lived experience of modernization.Week 8: Agrarian and Rural FuturesScreening: Moti Bagh (Nirmal Chander)Through a deeply personal portrayal of an aging farmer in Uttarakhand, Moti Bagh enables students to engage with agrarian policy, land use, rural development schemes, and environmentalsustainability. The film offersapoignant critique of the structural failures affecting Indian agriculture and raises questions about policy priorities and demographic transitions in rural India Week 9 Urban Policy This session will examine global housing inequality, displacement.and urban gentrification through a policy lens. Push exposes the collusion between multinational finance and local urban governance. illustrating how documentary films can critique neoliberal urbanplanning and advocate for housing as a right.Week 9-10 Documentary as an ethnographic Method for Public Policy This section introduces visual anthropology and the ethnographic filmtradition. Students will evaluate how ethnographic methods are adapted in documentary practices to investigate everyday life, rituals. and social structures. Core Screening: When Four Friends Meet allows a comparative discussion on genre, authorship, and reflexivity, while raisingquestions about representation, positionality, and subjectivity in public narratives. Discussions will focus on how ethnographic films can inform orcomplicate public understandings of social development policies, indigenous rights, and participatory governance. Week 11-12: Ethics, Representation in Documentary filmsThe course concludes with an in-depth look at the ethical dilemmas in documentary filmmaking. Students will interrogate the filmmaker`sresponsibility in representing trauma, marginality, and resistance. Key Screening: The Look of Silence (2014) by Joshua Oppenheimer serves as a focal point for discussions on truth-telling, reconciliation,and justice. Topics will include consent, agency, power asymmetries, and the documentary`s role in shaping historical memory and influencingpost-conflict policy. Conclusion: Documentary as Policy Intervention By the end of the course, students will have a comprehensive understanding of how documentary films function not just as art orreportage, but as powerful interventions in policy-making and public debate. Students will leave with the tools to analyze documentary cinema as a space where state, society, and storytelling converge.Evaluation: Attendance and Classroom Participation -20% End-Term Exam: Documentary Review Essay -25% Students will submit a critical review of two documentary films screened during the course, evaluating their policy relevance, aesthetic strategies, and impact. Emphasis should be on linking the films to broader contexts and course themes such as representation, governance, or development. Project Proposal & Treatment Note -30% Students will develop a concept note for a documentary idea aimed at a specific policy intervention (e.g., urban housing, education reform,environmental sustainability). Weekly Reflection Notes -25% (In-class/takehome) Students will submit short critical reflections (300-400 words) on five screenings across the semester (of their choice). These reflections should focus on linking form and content, and exploring the film`srelationship to state policy or public discourse.

Data science enables governments to optimize the allocation of public resources, evaluate the effectiveness of policies, and enhance service delivery across sectors such as health, education, and infrastructure. In addition to traditional econometric approaches, data science leverages advanced statistical and machine learning techniques to reach quicker and more precise results. Further, it facilitates cross-departmental insights, enabling departments to collaborate and share knowledge, leading to more holistic and impactful governance.Understanding the scope, methods, and applications of Data Science in Governance equips students of public policy with the means to analyse and manage large datasets, build models, track policy outcomes, generate actionable insights, and communicate these insights effectively. This course intends to bridge the gap between technical skills and policy analysis, fostering an understanding of the ethical and practical considerations involved in data use in governance, and ultimately supporting more responsive and inclusive governance practices. 1.
